description: Mapping the sky with right ascension, declination, altitude and azimuth — the two coordinate systems.
content_html:
The Celestial Sphere

Imagine the entire sky as the inside surface of an enormous hollow sphere, with Earth at its centre. Every star, planet and galaxy appears fixed to this surface at some angular position. This mental model is the celestial sphere. Even though stars are at vastly different distances, projecting them onto the sphere lets us describe angular positions without worrying about actual distances — extremely useful for navigation and observation planning.

The celestial sphere inherits key reference lines from Earth’s geography. Earth’s rotation axis, extended outward, meets the celestial sphere at the celestial poles. The north celestial pole (NCP) currently lies within 0.7° of the star Polaris. Earth’s equatorial plane, extended outward, creates the celestial equator, dividing the sky into northern and southern celestial hemispheres exactly as the geographic equator divides Earth.

Key Fact

The celestial sphere has poles directly above Earth’s geographic poles and an equator above Earth’s equator. The north celestial pole is marked (within 0.7°) by Polaris. All sky coordinates are measured as angles from these reference circles.

The Equatorial Coordinate System: RA and Dec

The equatorial coordinate system gives every star a permanent address on the celestial sphere, analogous to longitude and latitude on Earth:

  • Declination (Dec) is the celestial equivalent of latitude. It measures angular distance north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, in degrees, arcminutes and arcseconds. The celestial equator is Dec = 0°; the north celestial pole is Dec = +90°; the south celestial pole is Dec = −90°. Sirius has Dec = −16°43′; Polaris has Dec = +89°16′.
  • Right Ascension (RA) is the celestial equivalent of longitude. It is measured eastward from the First Point of Aries (the vernal equinox), the zero-point where the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator heading north. Unlike declination, RA is measured not in degrees but in hours, minutes and seconds of time (h, m, s), where 24 h = 360° and 1 h = 15°. This makes it easy to determine when a star crosses your meridian: if your local sidereal time is the same as a star’s RA, that star is on the meridian and at its highest.

Example coordinates: Betelgeuse is at RA 5 h 55 m, Dec +7°24′. The Pleiades cluster is at RA 3 h 47 m, Dec +24°7′. These coordinates are essentially fixed (they drift slowly due to precession over millennia, so star catalogues state an epoch such as J2000.0).

Because the Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, 1 hour of RA = 15°. Worked example: Betelgeuse at RA 5 h 55 m. Convert 5 h 55 m to degrees:

$$5 \text{ h} \times 15\degree/\text{h} = 75\degree$$ $$55 \text{ min} \times \frac{15\degree}{60 \text{ min}} = 13.75\degree$$ $$\text{Total RA} = 75\degree + 13.75\degree = 88.75\degree$$

This tells us Betelgeuse is 88.75° east of the First Point of Aries. Exam questions on the equatorial system sometimes ask you to perform this kind of conversion — show each step clearly.

The Horizon Coordinate System: Altitude and Azimuth

While equatorial coordinates are fixed to the stars, the horizon coordinate system (also called the altazimuth system) describes where an object appears right now from your specific location. It uses two angles:

  • Altitude is the angle in degrees above the observer’s horizon. The horizon is 0°; the zenith (directly overhead) is 90°. An object at altitude −5° is just below the horizon and not visible. Objects above 30° altitude are generally less affected by atmospheric extinction (absorption and scattering).
  • Azimuth is measured clockwise from north around the horizon. North = 0°; East = 90°; South = 180°; West = 270°. So a star at altitude 45°, azimuth 220° is in the south-south-west, about halfway up the sky.

Altitude and azimuth both change constantly as Earth rotates, so they depend on the observer’s latitude, longitude and the exact time. The same star that is at altitude 60° at midnight might be on the horizon six hours later. Altazimuth coordinates are therefore local and instantaneous, unlike RA and Dec which are fixed.

Key Fact

Altitude ranges from −90° (directly below) to +90° (zenith directly overhead). Azimuth is measured clockwise from north: North = 0°, East = 90°, South = 180°, West = 270°.

Linking the Two Coordinate Systems

To convert between RA/Dec and altitude/azimuth you need three things: the object’s RA and Dec, the observer’s latitude, and the local sidereal time (LST). The hour angle (HA) of a star is HA = LST − RA. A star rises in the east when HA is large and negative, transits the meridian (HA = 0) at its highest, and sets in the west as HA increases positively.

For the exam, you don’t need to perform the full spherical trigonometry conversion. But you do need to understand the conceptual link: a star with RA equal to the current LST is on the meridian and at its highest altitude. A star with RA six hours less than LST is six hours past the meridian, moving toward the western horizon. This relationship determines the best time to observe any target.

A target is highest in the sky, and therefore best placed for observation (least atmosphere to see through), when it transits the meridian. For a star at RA 6 h, transit occurs when the LST is 6 h. At the summer solstice, the Sun is around RA 6 h, meaning stars near RA 18 h are best placed at midnight. This is why Scorpius and Sagittarius (in the RA 17–20 h range) are summer midnight objects in the UK.

A useful rule: objects transit about four minutes earlier each night (because sidereal time gains four minutes per day on solar time). This means the whole RA range cycles through transit in one year — each constellation has its ‘season’ when it is highest and best placed at night.
exam_tip_html: Coordinate system questions are among the most difficult in this unit — candidates frequently mix up which system uses hours (equatorial RA) and which uses degrees only (altazimuth altitude and azimuth). Remember: RA is in hours (0–24 h, measured eastward from the First Point of Aries); Dec is in degrees (+90° to −90°); altitude is degrees above the horizon (0°–90°); azimuth is degrees clockwise from north (0°–360°). If asked to explain why altitude and azimuth change for the same star throughout the night, answer: because Earth’s rotation changes the observer’s orientation relative to the celestial sphere, while RA and Dec stay fixed.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The celestial sphere is an imaginary sphere centred on Earth with poles above the geographic poles and an equator above Earth’s equator; it provides a shared framework for sky coordinates.
  • Equatorial coordinates (RA in hours, Dec in degrees) are fixed to the stars and the same for all observers worldwide; altazimuth coordinates (altitude and azimuth, both in degrees) are local and change constantly with Earth’s rotation.
  • A star is best placed for observation when it transits the meridian (hour angle = 0, altitude is maximum); local sidereal time equals the RA of the star on the meridian.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes right ascension (RA)?
A) The angle of a star above the observer's horizon, measured in degrees
B) The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator, measured in degrees
C) The angle measured eastward along the celestial equator from the First Point of Aries, expressed in hours, minutes and seconds
D) The angle measured clockwise from north to a star around the observer's horizon
practice_questions.marks: C) The angle measured eastward along the celestial equator from the First Point of Aries, expressed in hours, minutes and seconds [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: State the azimuth of an object that is due south of an observer.

Caerwyn Observatory in Wales wants to observe the star Betelgeuse (RA 5 h 55 m, Dec +7°24'). Explain what the observer needs to know in order to determine the altitude and azimuth of Betelgeuse at a particular moment.
practice_questions.marks: The observer needs: the current local sidereal time (LST) [1 mark], to calculate the hour angle (HA = LST − RA), showing how far Betelgeuse is from the meridian [1 mark]; and the observer's geographic latitude [1 mark], since the altitude of a transiting object depends on (90° − latitude + declination).

practice_questions.text: A student measures the altitude of a star as 55° and its azimuth as 310°. In which direction does the star lie from the observer? Calculate how far the star is above the horizon.
practice_questions.marks: Azimuth 310° is north-north-west (between west at 270° and north at 360°) [1 mark]. The star is 55° above the horizon [1 mark]. (No calculation required for altitude — it is stated directly.)

practice_questions.text: Compare the equatorial coordinate system with the horizon coordinate system, giving two differences.
practice_questions.marks: Difference 1: Equatorial coordinates (RA and Dec) are fixed to the celestial sphere and do not change with the observer's location or the time of observation; altazimuth coordinates (altitude and azimuth) change continuously as Earth rotates and depend on the observer's latitude and longitude [1 mark each side = 2 marks]. Difference 2: RA is measured in hours (0–24 h) while azimuth is measured in degrees (0°–360°); both Dec and altitude are in degrees but Dec ranges ±90° while altitude ranges 0°–90° [1 mark each side = 2 marks].

practice_questions.text: Rosamund Vickers, an astronomy student in Glasgow (latitude 56°N), wants to observe a galaxy at declination +30°. Show that the galaxy reaches a maximum altitude of 64° when it transits the meridian at her location.
practice_questions.marks:
State formula: maximum altitude at transit = 90° − observer latitude + declination (for objects north of the zenith) [1 mark]. Or equivalently: altitude at transit = 90° − (latitude − declination) for Dec < latitude.
Substitute: 90° − 56° + 30° = 64° [1 mark for correct substitution, 1 mark for correct answer]. Units/statement: The galaxy is 64° above the horizon when on the meridian [1 mark].
(If student uses 90° − 56° + 30° correctly but makes an arithmetic error, 2 marks awarded for method.)

options: Hours, minutes and seconds of time
Degrees north or south of the celestial equator

The imaginary sphere of infinite radius centred on Earth, onto which all celestial objects appear projected, is called the _____ sphere.

right: Angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, in degrees

flashcard_questions.a: An imaginary sphere centred on Earth onto which all celestial objects are projected for measuring angular positions.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two equatorial coordinates of a star?
flashcard_questions.a: Right ascension (RA, in hours) and declination (Dec, in degrees).
Angular distance north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, measured in degrees.

flashcard_questions.q: What is right ascension measured from and in which direction?
flashcard_questions.a: Measured eastward from the First Point of Aries, in hours (0–24 h).

flashcard_questions.q: How many degrees does 1 hour of right ascension equal?
What are the two horizon coordinates?
flashcard_questions.a: Altitude (degrees above horizon) and azimuth (degrees clockwise from north).

flashcard_questions.q: What azimuth corresponds to due east?
Why do altitude and azimuth change throughout the night for the same star?
flashcard_questions.a: Earth's rotation changes the observer's orientation relative to the fixed celestial sphere.
The right ascension of the observer's meridian — the RA of whatever star is currently transiting.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the hour angle of a star on the meridian?
flashcard_questions.a: 0 hours — the star is at its highest altitude and best placed for observation.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two celestial coordinates of the north celestial pole?
flashcard_questions.a: RA is undefined (or any value); declination = +90°.

flashcard_questions.q: Which star marks the north celestial pole to within 0.7°?

glossary_terms.definition: An imaginary sphere of arbitrary large radius centred on Earth, onto which all celestial objects are projected for the purpose of describing their positions in the sky.
The two points on the celestial sphere directly above Earth's geographic North and South Poles, around which the entire sky appears to rotate.
The great circle on the celestial sphere lying directly above Earth's geographic equator, equidistant from the north and south celestial poles.
A coordinate system for the celestial sphere using right ascension and declination, fixed to the stars and independent of the observer's location on Earth.
A coordinate system centred on an individual observer that uses altitude above the horizon and azimuth measured clockwise from north to locate objects in the sky at a specific moment.
The current right ascension of the observer's meridian — equivalently, the hour angle of the First Point of Aries. When local sidereal time equals a star's RA, the star is crossing the meridian.
The angle, measured westward in hours from the observer's meridian to a celestial object, describing how far past the meridian the object currently is.

items.description: Veritasium explains how our position on the celestial sphere changes as Earth moves — great mental model for why RA and Dec are fixed while altitude/azimuth are not.

items.title: How Earth Moves
items.description: Shows Earth's rotation and orbit in detail — essential context for understanding how the celestial sphere appears to rotate once per sidereal day.

items.title: Hidden Figures (2016)
items.description: The story of NASA's human computers who worked out orbital mechanics by hand — coordinate systems and precise sky positioning were at the heart of their work.

items.description: Toggle between equatorial (RA/Dec) and horizon (Alt/Az) coordinates for any star in real time — see how altitude and azimuth change while RA and Dec stay fixed.

items.description: ROG explains the Prime Meridian, celestial equator and why Greenwich became the zero-point for both longitude and right ascension.

items.description: Clear tutorial on the equatorial coordinate system: how to read RA in hours and Dec in degrees, and how to use them to find objects.
